description: Width tiers for English Year 9 — 23 descriptors across Language, Literature and Literacy strands
subject: English

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest engagement that satisfies the descriptor's command term. One context, one example, one text — sufficient to demonstrate that the concept, skill or capability has been encountered. Not what is easy or common; what the descriptor demands at minimum.
width_notes.typical_width: Full engagement with the descriptor as ACARA intended it, grounded in the elaborations. Reflects sound practice across the range of examples the elaborations name. Does not require every elaboration but covers the scope and spirit of the descriptor.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that extend the range of contexts, phenomena, text types or analytical lenses — not harder versions of the same thing. Includes First Nations Australian directions where elaborations indicate them. May reasonably infer beyond elaborations within the descriptor's territory.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are the primary source for typical_width and wider. They are examples of how the descriptor might be addressed, not a required sequence. First Nations elaborations are treated as default wider directions.

AC9E9LA01.minimum_width: Identify language features that signal membership in one community and explain how they reinforce belonging.
AC9E9LA01.typical_width: Compare language features across multiple communities (family, peer group, classroom, online) explaining how each signals membership and reinforces identity; recognise how language reinforces roles as well as membership.
wider: Examine how First Nations Australian authors use language, including greetings in specific languages, to reinforce relationships to Country/Place and community — contrasting this with how mainstream texts construct community belonging
Analyse how jargon in technical online communities constructs hierarchies of expertise and positions newcomers as outsiders
Investigate how code-switching between community registers positions speakers differently depending on audience and setting
elaborations: identifying the various communities to which students belong and how language reinforces membership of these communities; for example, the intimate language of family members, the jargon of teenage groups, the technicality of some online communities, the language specific to recreational groups and the interaction patterns of the classroom
exploring language used by First Nations Australian authors to reinforce relationships to Country/Place and with others; for example, 'Hello' in Turrabul language is 'Galang nguruindhau'

AC9E9LA02.minimum_width: Identify one direct and one indirect evaluation in a text and explain how they differ in how they communicate the author's position.
AC9E9LA02.typical_width: Compare direct and indirect evaluation across multiple text types (print advertisements, editorials, talkback radio, podcasts, poetry) explaining how evocative vocabulary, similes and metaphors direct readers' views without explicit appraisal.
wider: Analyse how advertising systematically avoids direct evaluative claims while using evocative vocabulary and metaphor to position consumers
Examine how sustained metaphors in editorials construct an evaluative framework throughout a text — tracing how the vehicle imports connotations that guide interpretation
Compare how allusions to shared cultural references position readers who recognise them versus those who don't, as a mechanism of cultural evaluation
elaborations: comparing texts that use evaluative language in different ways; for example, print advertisements, editorials, talkback radio, podcasts and poetry, and identifying wording that appraises indirectly through evocative language, similes and metaphors that direct readers' views in particular ways

AC9E9LA03.minimum_width: Identify one text that departs from conventional structure for its genre and describe what the conventional structure would have been, explaining one effect of the departure.
AC9E9LA03.typical_width: Examine how authors adapt and subvert text structures across spoken, written, visual and multimodal elements — comparing linear and non-linear narratives, analysing opening paragraph structures in public texts, and evaluating the purpose and effect of different structural choices.
wider: Examine how digital and multimodal texts (interactive journalism, social media narratives) extend or subvert print conventions by making the navigation itself part of the structure
Analyse how spoken word poetry subverts conventions of both written poetry and spoken language simultaneously — operating as a hybrid that defamiliarises both modes
Compare how the same structural subversion device (e.g. in medias res opening) is used for different purposes across fiction, journalism and film
elaborations: comparing the use of linear and non-linear narratives in a range of short stories, and determining the purpose and effect of the different structures
comparing the opening paragraphs of different public texts such as feature articles, and determining the purpose and effect of the different structures and language features

AC9E9LA04.minimum_width: Identify text connectives in an argument and explain the logical relationship each signals; identify one nominalisation and explain what it condenses.
AC9E9LA04.typical_width: Investigate a range of cohesive devices including nominalisation and text connectives — examining how nominalisations condense prior argument and how connectives signal conclusion, reason and condition — across academic and technical texts.
wider: Analyse how nominalisation in political or bureaucratic texts obscures agency, and evaluate the effect on accountability — connecting cohesive device analysis to critical literacy
Compare the cohesive density of a student text with a published text, identifying where cohesive devices are underused and explaining the effect on coherence
Investigate how connective choices shade the logical force of a claim — comparing 'however', 'nevertheless' and 'despite this' in academic argument contexts
elaborations: sequencing and developing an argument using language structures that suggest conclusions ('therefore', 'moreover' and 'so') or give reasons ('since', 'because') or suggest conditionals ('if … then')

AC9E9LA05.minimum_width: Identify one deliberate structural violation (fragment, stand-alone dependent clause or interrupting clause) and explain why it is intentional and what effect it creates.
AC9E9LA05.typical_width: Identify and analyse how authors use deliberate sentence violations — fragments, stand-alone dependent clauses, interrupting clauses — across literary, journalistic and advertising texts, explaining effects of emphasis, rhythm, voice and immediacy.
wider: Compare how structural violations in literary fiction versus advertising create different effects and reflect different community tolerances for deviation from standard conventions
Examine how interrupting clauses are used to mimic the rhythms of thought in stream-of-consciousness or first-person narrative — tracing how the device constructs interiority
Analyse how a specific author's characteristic use of sentence violation contributes to their distinctive prose style
elaborations: identifying the effects of using an interrupting clause inside another clause; for example, 'His friend, who had left home the previous year, suddenly returned.', intentionally using a dependent clause on its own; for example, 'If you see what I mean.' or using a sentence fragment; for example, 'Breathtaking!'

AC9E9LA06.minimum_width: Identify two abstract nouns used as summary references in a text and explain what each condenses from earlier content.
AC9E9LA06.typical_width: Analyse how abstract nouns and nominalisation condense, structure and carry forward arguments in academic and technical texts — examining how nominalisations transform processes into things that can be positioned and qualified in subsequent argument.
wider: Compare how abstract nouns and nominalisation function differently in scientific versus humanistic writing, examining what each reveals about how different disciplines build knowledge through condensing
Examine how nominalisation can obscure who is doing what, and evaluate the ideological implications of agency-erasure in journalism or political discourse
elaborations: exploring sections of academic and technical texts, and analysing the use of abstract nouns; for example, 'the previous argument', 'the prologue', to summarise and distil information, structure the argument and summarise preceding explanations

AC9E9LA07.minimum_width: Identify one visual symbol in a still or moving image and explain the meaning it contributes beyond its literal presence.
AC9E9LA07.typical_width: Analyse how specific symbols — seasons, weather, colours — augment meaning in still images, films and picture books, evaluating their contribution to viewer understanding; recognise that visual symbols carry different meanings for different groups and cultures.
wider: Examine how First Nations Australian visual art uses symbols that may have multiple layered meanings or different meanings across different Nations/communities — contrasting this with the more fixed symbolic conventions of mainstream Western visual texts
Compare how the same visual symbol carries different connotations across cultural contexts, identifying where symbolic meanings are shared and where they diverge significantly
Analyse how a recurring visual symbol in a film accumulates and transforms meaning across its duration
elaborations: investigating the use of symbols; for example, specific seasons, weather and colours in images, films and picture books, and evaluating their contribution to viewers' understanding, recognising that visual and verbal symbols have different meanings for different groups and cultures

understanding the use of symbols by First Nations Australians, where a symbol may have many meanings or have different meanings across First Nations Australian groups; for example, artwork enables First Nations Australians from a particular Country/Place to identify symbols and interpret the artwork

AC9E9LA08.minimum_width: Identify vocabulary choices in a text that create a recognisable tone and explain how the connotations of those words produce that tone.
AC9E9LA08.typical_width: Analyse how vocabulary choices contribute to style, mood and tone across a range of texts — identifying words that create sarcastic tone, explaining how vocabulary builds stylistic effectiveness, and distinguishing the separate effects of tone (author attitude) and mood (reader atmosphere).
wider: Compare vocabulary styles across two texts by the same author, identifying consistent stylistic markers and evaluating what they contribute to the author's recognisable voice
Compare how the same subject is treated with different tonal registers in two texts (e.g. news report vs satirical piece), analysing which specific vocabulary shifts produce the tonal difference
Examine how culturally specific vocabulary signals register and community membership — connecting vocabulary analysis to the language and identity strand (AC9E9LA01)
elaborations: identifying the words used to create nuanced meaning; for example, identifying the words that create a sarcastic tone in a text
identifying how the vocabulary used in a text contributes to its stylistic effectiveness

AC9E9LA09.minimum_width: Apply correct punctuation for at least two direct quotations in a piece of writing, and make one justified decision about whether to quote directly or paraphrase.
AC9E9LA09.typical_width: Understand and apply punctuation conventions for direct quotation, paraphrase and general source reporting across essays, reviews and academic assignments — including decisions about when each attribution form is appropriate.
wider: Compare how different citation conventions (APA, MLA, Chicago) handle quotation punctuation and attribution, examining why standardisation matters in academic contexts
Analyse how journalistic attribution conventions differ from academic ones — examining different relationships to source identity, verification and authority

Limited width: punctuation conventions for citation are relatively fixed within the year band. Extension goes toward genre variation in attribution practices rather than significant contextual widening.
elaborations: understanding who to and how to cite in essays, reviews and academic assignments, and when it is appropriate to use direct quotations or to report sources more generally

AC9E9LE01.minimum_width: Identify authorial choices in the representation of one character or place and explain how at least one choice reflects a contextual factor.
AC9E9LE01.typical_width: Analyse representations of people and places in literary texts from different historical, social and cultural contexts — exploring values associated with authority, community and family across cultures and times; examining how First Nations Australian authors reflect unique ways of being, knowing and doing.
wider: Explore how wide-ranging Australian novels, poems and films represent water and characters' relationships with water — tracing how this recurring motif is contextually inflected differently across texts and time periods

Compare representations of the same type of person or community (e.g. rural Australia, immigrant experience) across texts from different time periods, examining how changing contexts produce different representations
Examine how First Nations Australian literary texts construct representations that resist or respond to mainstream Australian representational conventions
elaborations: exploring and comparing representations of values of characters; for example, exploring the values associated with authority, community and family in literature drawn from different cultures and times
exploring how texts by First Nations Australian authors reflect unique ways of being, knowing, thinking and doing
exploring the way wide-ranging Australian novels, poems and films represent water and characters' relationships with water

AC9E9LE02.minimum_width: Articulate an initial response to a literary text and make one comparison with a subsequent analytical observation — explaining what changed between first impression and closer reading.
AC9E9LE02.typical_width: Present a personal response that traces the journey from initial impressions to developed whole-text analysis — interrogating and making judgements about the text, comparing others' ideas against the student's own, and reaching an independent or considered position.
wider: Read a text a second time and reflect on how knowledge of the ending changes the interpretation of earlier sections — examining how re-reading reveals what the first-read missed
Compare your interpretation of a text's central ideas against a published review, explaining points of agreement, disagreement and the reasoning behind divergences
Examine how sharing initial responses with peers before detailed analysis changes subsequent interpretation — reflecting on reading as a social and dialogic process
elaborations: interrogating and making judgements about a text, comparing others' ideas against the student's own and reaching an independent decision or consensus about the interpretations and ideas expressed

AC9E9LE03.minimum_width: Identify at least two literary features that create a personal preference response and explain how each shapes the response.
AC9E9LE03.typical_width: Reflect on and discuss literary responses — connecting characterisation, setting, plot events, themes and literary devices to preference factors — and collaboratively formulate criteria for what distinguishes literary value.
wider: Compare criteria for literary value developed collaboratively in class with criteria used in published literary awards or reviews, identifying overlaps and examining gaps
Examine how different cultural communities hold different criteria for literary value, and what this reveals about the relationship between culture and aesthetic judgement
Survey peer preferences for the same text and analyse which features create different responses — examining whether preference factors are personal, cultural or conventional
elaborations: reflecting on and discussing responses to literature including characterisation, setting details, plot events, themes and literary devices used to achieve particular effects, and collaboratively formulating a list of factors that distinguish value

AC9E9LE04.minimum_width: Identify at least two consistent stylistic features across two texts by the same author and evaluate the aesthetic appeal of one aspect of the style.
AC9E9LE04.typical_width: Compare texts by the same author to determine literary style — examining vocabulary patterns, sentence structure and narrative technique — and evaluate the aesthetic qualities and appeal, assessing their distinctiveness and presenting comparisons to others.
wider: Compare how cultural background and context shape what readers find aesthetically appealing in literary style, examining where aesthetic preferences are culturally situated
Examine how an author's style evolved over their career and evaluate what drove the evolution — tracing consistency and change in the aesthetic signature
Compare an author who writes in multiple genres and examine what remains stylistically consistent versus what adapts to genre expectations
elaborations: comparing texts created by the same author to determine literary style, assessing their appeal and presenting comparisons to others

AC9E9LE05.minimum_width: Identify one complex literary device (extended metaphor, allegory, metonymy, symbolism or intertextual reference) and explain the effect it creates by importing meaning from outside the immediate statement.
AC9E9LE05.typical_width: Analyse the effect of text structures, language features and literary devices — extended metaphor, metonymy, allegory, symbolism and intertextual references — examining how imagery and devices contribute to meaning and influence emotional responses across poems and prose texts.
wider: Analyse how a text deploys allegory and symbolism simultaneously, tracing how the two systems of meaning support or complicate each other

Examine how intertextual references create two-tier reading experiences (for readers who recognise versus those who don't), and evaluate the implications for authorial choice and audience construction

Compare how First Nations Australian storytelling traditions use symbolism in ways that carry specific cultural knowledge that may be inaccessible to outsiders — examining what this reveals about the cultural situatedness of symbolic meaning systems
elaborations: examining how different authors make use of devices such as imagery, and explaining the effect of these choices on audiences
identifying examples of literary devices in a range of poems and considering how they contribute to meaning and influence the emotional responses of the audience

AC9E9LE06.minimum_width: Create and draft a short literary text with one deliberate structural experiment, and edit for at least one coherence issue.
AC9E9LE06.typical_width: Create and edit literary texts — potentially hybrid — experimenting with text structures, language features and literary devices; adapt existing texts through prequel, sequel or form transformation; edit for run-on sentences, purposeful detail and linked paragraphs.
wider: Take an existing short story, poem, play or speech and create a short film or multimodal adaptation — examining what must change and what can be preserved across the medium transformation
Engage in iterative peer editing with explicit criteria for whether structural and device experiments are achieving their stated purpose — developing evaluative criteria for creative revision
Adapt a traditional or contemporary text and reflect on how the original text constrained and enabled the new one — examining the creative and intertextual dialogue between versions
elaborations: taking an existing short story, poem, play or speech in print form and creating a short film
adapting traditional and contemporary literature through textual intervention, prequel or sequel
editing by checking for run-on sentences, ensuring that detail or repetition is used for effect, and ensuring paragraphs are linked in ways that develop the narrative

AC9E9LY01.minimum_width: Identify two representations of the same subject from different contexts and explain one contextual factor that produces the difference.
AC9E9LY01.typical_width: Examine how representations of public figures in media vary across different contexts; analyse how news is conveyed and how language features represent individuals or groups; compare texts from different time periods.
wider: Compare how a news event is represented in media from different national contexts, examining how national perspective shapes framing and what this reveals about the relationship between context and representation
Analyse how language that was normalised in historical texts to represent a group is recognised as problematic today — tracing how changing contexts alter representational norms
Examine how the same abstract concept ('progress', 'freedom', 'tradition') is represented differently across texts from different political or cultural contexts
elaborations: examining the representation of public figures in media and recognising how these vary in different contexts
identifying and analysing how news is conveyed in texts; for example, analysing representations of an event at a particular time reported in the media
comparing texts from different time periods and analysing the language features used to represent individuals or groups

AC9E9LY02.minimum_width: Identify two language features in a spoken text and explain how each positions the listener; present an opinion about the text with at least one specific feature as evidence.
AC9E9LY02.typical_width: Analyse how language features position listeners in spoken texts with different purposes and audiences — examining stereotype creation and how language directs response; use effective dialogue strategies in formal and informal discussion contexts.
wider: Compare how the same topic positions listeners differently in two spoken texts from different contexts (community radio vs commercial broadcast) — analysing how context shapes the positioning mechanisms used
Examine how podcasts use para-linguistic features alongside language to create intimacy and position the listener as an in-group member
Conduct a formal discussion of a spoken text and evaluate how the structured dialogue format affects the quality of opinion exchange
elaborations: discussing how stereotypes are created through language and how they position listeners to respond

using effective strategies for dialogue and discussion in a range of formal and informal contexts, including speaking clearly and coherently and for an appropriate length of time, presenting an opinion and listening to the opinions of others

AC9E9LY03.minimum_width: Identify two language features in a text and analyse how each represents a particular perspective on the subject.
AC9E9LY03.typical_width: Analyse and evaluate how language features represent perspectives across news and social media, editorial writing, and advocacy or inspirational speeches — making supported judgements about the effectiveness and fairness of the representation.
wider: Compare language features across coverage of the same contentious issue in two publications with different editorial positions — mapping how language choices embed different perspective-representations
Evaluate how language in advocacy speeches from films or media influences the listener, assessing both the effectiveness and ethical dimensions of the techniques used
Analyse how language in historical texts represents a group in ways now recognised as problematic, and assess the ongoing impact of such representations
elaborations: analysing the use of language in the coverage of a contentious issue in a range of news and social media
explaining how authors use language features to represent ideas and convey opinions
comparing a range of advocacy, campaign or inspirational speeches from films or media and identifying language features that influence the listener

AC9E9LY04.minimum_width: Identify two organisational techniques in a text and evaluate the impact of one on meaning.
AC9E9LY04.typical_width: Analyse and evaluate techniques used in texts to organise ideas and evoke emotional responses — comparison, contrast, exaggeration, juxtaposition, chronological manipulation, expansion and compression of time — explaining whether the author conveys meaning effectively through the arrangement.
wider: Reorder a section of a text and evaluate how the reorganisation changes the meaning or emotional impact — using the exercise to illuminate the significance of the original organisational choices
Compare how two texts covering the same event use different organisational techniques, assessing which arrangement is more effective for each text's purpose
Evaluate the organisational coherence of a student text and provide targeted developmental feedback on one structural improvement
elaborations: evaluating techniques used in texts to organise ideas and evoke emotional responses, such as comparison, contrast, exaggeration, juxtaposition, the changing of chronological order, and the expansion and compression of time
explaining whether the author conveys meaning effectively, through the sequence of information and evidence

AC9E9LY05.minimum_width: Apply at least two comprehension strategies to compare ideas or opinions in two texts, explaining how each strategy supported the comparison.
AC9E9LY05.typical_width: Use a range of comprehension strategies — visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring, questioning, inferring — to compare and contrast visual and print/digital representations of ideas, current events and opinions across texts.
wider: Apply comprehension strategies to compare texts with conflicting interpretations of the same event, evaluating the quality of evidence each presents and mapping the ideological positions on offer
Compare visual representations of the same issue across online news sources and evaluate how visual choices support or contradict the verbal argument
Develop a comparison protocol for a specific text type pair (e.g. broadsheet vs social media on same event), identifying which comprehension strategies are most productive for each pairing
elaborations: comparing and contrasting visual representations of ideas, issues or events in online news reporting
comparing the representation of an event in print and digital sources, summarising their qualities, identifying opinions and analysing evidence
summarising articles representing a current event comparing and contrasting ideas and opinions in and between texts

AC9E9LY06.minimum_width: Plan and draft a text with a clear contention and two supporting points; create with at least one deliberate structural and language choice; edit for one accuracy and one effectiveness issue.
AC9E9LY06.typical_width: Plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts across argumentative, analytical and informative purposes — developing linked argument structure, selecting language features and literary devices, using precise vocabulary, and editing for accuracy and clarity.
wider: Create a text that deliberately subverts a conventional structure for this text type, and evaluate the effect of the structural experiment on purpose and audience
Develop a personal editing checklist calibrated to your own known error patterns, and apply it systematically across a substantial draft
Create a multimodal text and evaluate how multimodal choices expand or complicate what could be achieved in written mode alone — examining the affordances of different modes
elaborations: developing an argument that has a series of sequenced and linked paragraphs, beginning with a contention, followed by a series of supported points that develop a line of argument, and a conclusion that summarises the main line of argument
creating informative texts that explain and analyse complex phenomena using well-chosen facts and precise language

reviewing and editing their own and others' texts, which may involve using online applications, for accuracy of grammar, spelling and punctuation, and to achieve particular purposes and address specific audiences by improving clarity and control of content through organising, developing, extending and linking ideas
discussing choices of literary devices used in a literary text with a peer, and evaluating the potential effect of each choice on an audience

AC9E9LY07.minimum_width: Plan and deliver a spoken presentation with a clear purpose and structure, demonstrating deliberate use of at least one voice feature and one language or device choice.
AC9E9LY07.typical_width: Plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations across informative, persuasive, analytical and imaginative purposes — selecting voice features for effect, adapting literary devices to meet audience needs, using graphics and animations, and collaborating in group presentations.
wider: Create and deliver a news-style current affairs presentation integrating images with spoken text to influence viewer response, then evaluate how effectively the multimodal combination achieved the stated purpose
Collaborate with peers to develop and deliver an imaginative recreation of part of a text, reflecting on how group delivery decisions collectively represent a key idea
Compare planning strategies for a formal seminar versus a debate, identifying what structural decisions differ and examining why the different forms demand different organisation
elaborations: using graphics and text animations to accompany spoken text; for example, presenting a news item suitable for a current affairs program that uses images with spoken text to influence a viewer's response
selecting features of voice such as tone, volume, pitch and pace for their specific effects to create tone or to persuade an audience

choosing text structures and adapting literary devices such as similes, metaphors and personification to meet the perceived needs of an audience when debating a topic, creating a voiceover for a media presentation or presenting a seminar
collaborating with peers to develop imaginative recreations of part of a text or to represent a key idea in a text

AC9E9LY08.minimum_width: Identify one example of deliberate spelling variation in a text and explain what characterisation, humour or accent effect it creates.
AC9E9LY08.typical_width: Understand how spelling is used in texts for effects including characterisation, humour, neologism and accent representation — analysing dropped letters emulating spoken speech, exploring neologisms like 'selfie' and 'Paralympics', and explaining how spelling choices signal register and community membership.
wider: Compare how different authors represent similar accents or dialect through spelling — examining the range of conventions and evaluating what is gained or risked, including the ethics of representing communities through non-standard spelling
Trace how a digital neologism entered mainstream usage, examining how its spelling and form stabilised or shifted as it moved from subculture into general use
Compare how intentional misspelling functions in advertising versus social media — examining what different communities accept as humorous versus offensive, and why
elaborations: exploring the spelling of neologisms and their effect in media texts such as online posts; for example, 'selfie' and 'Paralympics'
analysing how spelling is used to represent the distinctive speech of a character by noting where authors have dropped letters from words to emulate the sound of spoken words
